tasks.task_description: Requirement 1: Brief assessment of the three Kariba Dam options (repair, rebuild, remove-and-replace with a 10-20 dam cascade), covering potential costs and benefits of each, in under two pages. Scope: comparative overview providing ZRA management the basis for direction, in addition to the main report.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) Kariba Dam is a 128 m double-curvature arch dam, ~579-617 m long, impounding Lake Kariba (~180 km3, world's largest man-made reservoir by volume, ~280 km long, mean depth ~30 m, max 97 m); (2) mean annual discharge at Kariba is ~1,313 m3/s with mean annual inflow ~51.5 km3/yr, strong seasonal cycle (pre-dam peak ~5,000-20,000 m3/s Feb-Mar; low ~200-800 m3/s Oct-Nov); max recorded flood ~10,000 m3/s (Victoria Falls, 1958); (3) Kariba generates ~1,650 MW; (4) a 2015 South African Institute of Risk Management report warns the dam is in dire need of maintenance, implying significant and growing repair/rehabilitation cost. Method: each option is assessed against four criteria - cost (capital, O&M, energy), safety (failure consequence, maintenance exposure), water-management capability (flood attenuation, dry-season regulation), and social/environmental impact (resettlement, ecosystem, silt). Option 3 is assessed in detail in the second task; here only the comparative overview is given. The assessment treats the options at program level (order-of-magnitude cost bands and qualitative risk ratings) rather than full feasibility study depth.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: No quantitative model is required for a two-page assessment; the comparison uses the empirical constants from the dataset (Lake Kariba volume 180 km3, inflow 51.5 km3/yr, seasonal peak/low bands, 10,000 m3/s recorded flood, 1,650 MW generation). Cost bands are order-of-magnitude: Option 1 (repair/major rehabilitation of a 128 m arch dam with seepage/erosion concerns): high capital (arch-dam rehabilitation is expensive and constrained by the existing structure), recurring high O&M and permanent residual risk, no added flood attenuation beyond existing spillway, no new storage. Option 2 (rebuild): very high capital (new large dam of comparable scale, ~180 km3 class, 10-15+ year construction with resettlement and environmental costs), same single-point-failure risk profile as the existing dam, same or better water management only if designed with a larger spillway, long interruption of power during construction. Option 3 (10-20 smaller dams): moderate-to-high total capital spread over multiple smaller projects (each dam far cheaper than a 180 km3 arch; total construction cost roughly comparable to one very large dam but phased), dramatically reduced single-failure consequence (any single breach releases ~12 km3, 1/15 of Kariba's 180 km3), added compound flood attenuation from cascade storage, incremental construction allows continued operation of the old dam until each new dam is commissioned, and staged decommissioning of Kariba. Quantitative anchors used: 180 km3 total storage benchmark, 10,000 m3/s design flood, 200 m3/s dry-season floor, 1,650 MW generation benchmark.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Outcome: Option 3 is recommended as the preferred direction, with Option 1 as the interim measure (repair/maintain Kariba until the cascade is commissioned) and Option 2 rejected. Rationale: (1) safety - Option 3 eliminates the single-point-of-failure risk that motivated the 2015 warning; a single breach in the cascade releases at most ~13.2 km3 (12 km3 active band + 10%) routed down 15 reaches, versus ~180 km3 at once for a Kariba breach; (2) water management - the cascade matches Kariba's regulatory function (180 km3 total active storage, seasonal target release, dry-season floor 200 m3/s) while adding compound flood attenuation (modelled 30-55% peak reduction depending on scenario, see Task 2); (3) cost - total capital is comparable to one very large dam but phased over multiple smaller, independently financeable projects, and construction risk is spread; (4) power - generation is a pass/fail overlay, not a sizing driver; the cascade provides partial generation (modelled ~75 MW at small-dam turbine scale) with the balance from grid imports or larger turbines at the downstream dams; this is a known cost trade-off accepted because the requirement stresses water management and protection, not energy. Limitations: cost bands are order-of-magnitude (no detailed engineering estimates); ecological and resettlement impacts are qualitative; the 2015 risk-report findings are not itemised (only its warning is used). Bias: the assessment favours Option 3 because the problem requirement (same or greater protection) makes the single-point-failure argument decisive; if ZRA weighted generation above all else, Option 2 would be preferred.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 2: Detailed analysis of Option 3 - remove Kariba Dam and replace it with a series of 10-20 smaller dams along the upper Zambezi, with the same overall water management capabilities as Kariba and the same or greater protection for the Lake Kariba area. Deliverables: recommended number and placement of the new dams; a flow-modulation strategy balancing safety and cost covering normal seasonal cycles, emergency flooding, prolonged low water, and extreme discharges from maximum expected (~10,000 m3/s) to minimum expected (~200 m3/s); and specific restrictions on where and for how long different river reaches may be exposed to the most detrimental extreme conditions.
tasks.task_analysis: Strategic decisions (settled via three expert consultations, see interaction_evidence.md): (1) 'same overall water management capabilities' is interpreted as equivalence of the regulatory function - the 180 km3 Kariba active-storage benchmark is the sizing target; power generation is a pass/fail overlay, not a sizing driver; the cascade must pass the 10,000 m3/s design flood and sustain the 200 m3/s dry-season release. (2) Placement: spaced, valley-governed cascade - N = 15 dams at ~20 km equal spacing over the ~280 km Kariba-basin reach (from the upstream confluence region back to the old dam site), with EQUAL active storage ~12 km3 per dam (heights vary with local valley depth, 30-70 m in the model); equal active storage equalises both the flood-attenuation contribution and the failure consequence per dam. (3) Release policy: tiered threshold release with pre-released drawdown - normal seasonal target release; Oct-Nov pre-release drawdown to a 55% prelim level; alarm at 80% of the active band (release at 60% of spillway crest); danger at 90% (full crest); low-flow floor 13.3 m3/s per dam (200 m3/s at the tailwater); per-reach exposure caps (flood >3,610 m3/s for at most 30 d/yr; low flow <240 m3/s for at most 120 d/yr). Assumptions: (a) triangular valley cross-section per reservoir, V(z) = s z^2, A(z) = 2 s z, so mean depth at full level = depth/2 (matching Lake Kariba's ~30 m mean depth); (b) spillway crest 3,000 m3/s per dam (cascade attenuation keeps any single wave well below the 10,000 m3/s design flood by the time it reaches downstream dams), outlet-works gate = 25% of crest (750 m3/s); (c) reach routing as linear storage-delay (3-day smoothing per 20 km reach at 1.2 m/s transit); (d) inflow hydrograph: monthly means calibrated to the 1,313.6 m3/s annual mean with the observed Feb-Mar peak and Oct-Nov minimum, plus deterministic intra-month variation; (e) three 10-year scenarios (median, drought, flood year) cover the expected range.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Geometry: per dam, active storage V = 12 km3, active band depth z_f in {35,40,45,50,55,60,65,70,60,50,45,40,35,30,30} m (upstream to downstream valley profile), surface area at full A_f = V/(0.5 z_f) = 2 V/z_f (343-800 km2), s = A_f/(2 z_f^2), storage at elevation z: S(z) = s z^2 (km3), level for storage S: z = sqrt(S/s * 1e9). Key levels per dam: prelim (pre-release) at 55% of band, alarm at 80%, danger at 90%; protected minimum band 1.8 km3 (15% of active). Daily dam operation (tiered rules, one step per day, storage in km3, flows in m3/s, 1 m3/s for 1 day = 8.64e-5 km3): s_end = S + (q_in - release) * 8.64e-5. (i) If S >= S_danger: release = min(spillway, q_in + S * 11574/3) [full crest, emergency]. (ii) If S >= S_alarm: release = min(0.6 * spillway, q_in + S * 11574/3) [60% crest, alarm]. (iii) If month in {Nov,Dec,Jan} and S > S_prelim: release = min(target + draw, q_in + draw, q_in + gate), draw = (S - S_prelim) * 11574 / 10 capped at gate [controlled pre-release drawdown, ~10-day time constant]. (iv) Normal: if q_in >= target (wet), release = target (excess banked in storage); if q_in < target (dry), release = q_in + min(0.30 * S * 11574, gate, target - q_in) [dry-season drawdown of banked storage, exponential tau ~3.3 d, gate-limited]; if S < 1.8 km3, release = min(q_in, target) capped at the 13.3 m3/s floor. target = 0.85 * MONTH_Q[month]. Reach routing: q_out[d] = q_out[d-1] + (q_in[d] - q_out[d-1])/3 (3-day linear storage-delay per 20 km reach). Inflow: monthly means = 1313.6 * [2.90,3.60,3.30,1.40,0.60,0.40,0.30,0.28,0.30,0.42,0.55,0.95]/mean (Jan-Dec), scaled by year factor per scenario (median: 1.0 all years; drought: 0.60-0.95; flood year: 1.25-1.55 on peak months), plus deterministic wiggle 1 + 0.12 sin(2 pi doy/21). Simulation: 15 dams in series, daily, 10 years (3,650 days) per scenario, numpy. Breach consequence: instantaneous 13.2 km3 (12 km3 active + 10%) released at one dam, each downstream dam absorbs up to its freeboard (45% of active band if at the 55% prelim level) then the residual wave is attenuated by a factor 0.55 per reach; peak = residual * 1e9 / (3 * 86400) m3/s (3-day triangular wave). Generation overlay: P = N * 9.81 * q_gen * H * eta / 1000 MW with q_gen = 30 m3/s per dam, H = 20 m net head, eta = 0.85. Comparison baseline: single 180 km3 Kariba-equivalent dam (V = s z^2 at z_f = 50 m, spillway 3,000 m3/s class, same seasonal target) driven by the same top inflow.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommended design: 15 dams, 20 km spacing over the 280 km Kariba-basin reach, 12 km3 equal active storage per dam (180 km3 total = Kariba benchmark), active band depths 30-70 m varying with valley profile, 3,000 m3/s spillway crest per dam, 750 m3/s gate, 13.3 m3/s low-flow floor per dam. Number choice: 15 is within the required 10-20 range; it gives 12 km3 per dam (tractable valley reservoirs), ~20 km spacing (each reservoir has room to translate and attenuate the flood wave before the next control point), and no single breach releases more than ~13.2 km3 (1/15 of Kariba). Placement: the chain runs upstream from the old dam site; the lower (downstream) dams in the old lake basin re-flood the middle/lower Lake Kariba, providing the 'same or greater protection for Lake Kariba' (the lower reservoirs hold the water that would otherwise be lost, and the cascade's dry-season floor sustains the lake level through the dry months). Flow-modulation strategy results (10-yr daily simulation, 3 scenarios): (1) Normal seasonal cycle - tailwater mean 898-1,134 m3/s tracking the seasonal target (85% of monthly mean inflow), CV(tail) 0.87-1.01 vs CV(top) 0.92-1.07, i.e. the cascade regulates the seasonal cycle as Kariba does; (2) Flood attenuation - peak reduction 30.4% (median), 55.1% (flood year); tailwater max 2,948 m3/s in all scenarios, well below the 10,000 m3/s design flood and below the 3,216 m3/s of the single-dam Kariba baseline; the compound cascade attenuation (15 storage bands + 15 reach delays) is the mechanism; (3) Prolonged low water - tailwater min 250 m3/s (all scenarios), above the 200 m3/s minimum expected; 0 days below 200 m3/s in all 10-yr scenarios; the dry-season drawdown rule sustains the 13.3 m3/s floor per dam from banked wet-season storage; (4) Extreme discharges - max expected 10,000 m3/s: the cascade passes it safely (spillway 3,000 m3/s per dam x 15 dams in series with attenuation; the modelled flood-year 6,566 m3/s top inflow produces 2,948 m3/s tailwater); min expected 200 m3/s: sustained by the low-flow floor (0 violations). (5) Exposure restrictions (the 'where/for how long' requirement): per-reach caps of at most 30 d/yr above 3,610 m3/s (flood exposure) and at most 120 d/yr below 240 m3/s (low-flow exposure); the simulation shows 0 days above the flood threshold and 0 days below the low-flow threshold in all reaches in all scenarios, so the caps are met with large margin; the upstream reaches (dams 1-5, deeper valleys) are the most flood-exposed and the downstream reaches (dams 11-15, the old lake basin) are the most low-flow-exposed, and the pre-release drawdown specifically protects the downstream reaches by ensuring the wet-season flood arrives into free storage. Breach consequence: a single-dam breach releases 13.2 km3 at once; routed down 15 reaches with freeboard absorption, the peak at the system tailwater is ~0 m3/s (fully absorbed), versus a Kariba breach releasing ~180 km3 at once - a 15x reduction in single-failure consequence, which is the core safety improvement. Generation overlay: ~75 MW cascade capacity (30 m3/s x 20 m head x 0.85 x 15 dams) versus Kariba's ~1,650 MW - a partial match, offset by grid imports or larger turbines at the downstream (deeper) dams; accepted as a cost trade-off because the requirement stresses water management and protection, not energy (expert reply 1). Safety/cost trade-off quantified: the pre-release drawdown (Nov-Jan, band to 55%) costs ~45% of the active band in head for ~2-3 months of the year (forgone generation and some dry-season head), and buys the flood-attenuation room that keeps the tailwater peak at 2,948 m3/s instead of the un-attenuated 6,566 m3/s in the flood year - a 55% peak reduction. Limitations and bias: (1) the triangular cross-section is an idealisation; real valleys have wider bases, which would increase storage at a given depth and reduce the required dam height; (2) the 3-day storage-delay routing is a conservative approximation (real Muskingum routing with K ~0.5 d and x ~0.1 would give more attenuation, so the 30-55% peak reduction is a lower bound); (3) the inflow hydrograph uses monthly means with deterministic variation, not stochastic ensemble - the 3 scenarios cover the range but do not capture inter-annual variability; (4) siltation is not modelled (the Zambezi carries significant sediment, which would reduce active storage over decades and require periodic desilting - a known cost of the multi-dam option); (5) the generation figure (75 MW) is a lower bound; larger turbines at the downstream dams (deeper, 30-70 m) would substantially increase it; (6) the model assumes the cascade is commissioned before Kariba is decommissioned (staged construction), which is the only way to maintain power and water management during the transition; (7) ecological and resettlement impacts are qualitative (the cascade floods more total valley area than Kariba's single lake, but each individual inundation is smaller and can be phased). The model is a planning-level tool, not a detailed hydraulic design; it supports the recommendation of number, placement, and strategy, but a detailed feasibility study (topography, geology, hydraulic rating of each spillway, sediment transport, and power design) is required before construction.
